::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Start here

This is a **self-contained, runnable tutorial**. There is no prerequisite reading
and nothing to buy: every idea is introduced briefly, then *demonstrated* in a
short Python notebook you can open, run, and modify. If you can read `numpy`, you
can follow along.
:::

## Why learn this

The same simple move — averaging over random quantum evolution — has quietly become
one of the most productive ideas in modern physics, and it turns up in places that
look completely unrelated:

- **Why isolated quantum systems thermalize.** A closed system never forgets its
  initial state, yet any small part of it settles to something that looks thermal.
  Typicality is the reason, and it underlies the modern understanding of quantum
  statistical mechanics.
- **The black-hole information problem.** How information that falls into a black
  hole re-emerges in its radiation is, in the end, the same Page-curve calculation
  you will do here. Scrambling is the concrete bridge between quantum gravity and
  quantum information.
- **Whether quantum computers do what they claim.** The benchmarks that certify real
  hardware — randomized benchmarking, cross-entropy, classical shadows — all rest on
  Haar randomness. This is not abstract: it is how groups at Google and IBM
  characterize their chips.
- **The limits of quantum machine learning.** The barren-plateau problem, which stops
  many quantum models from training at all, is the same concentration of measure seen
  from another angle. Understanding it tells you which quantum-ML ideas can work
  before you write a line of code.

Few subjects sit at the meeting point of high-energy theory, condensed matter, quantum
information, and machine learning. This one does — and the core toolkit is small enough
to learn in a few focused sittings, yet general enough to reuse for the rest of your
research. Learning to compute a Haar average by hand is a genuinely transferable skill.

## What you'll learn

A surprising amount of modern quantum theory rests on a single question: **what
happens when you average over random quantum evolutions?** The answer ties
together topics that look unrelated at first —

> spectral statistics of chaotic Hamiltonians · the entanglement of a typical
> quantum state · how scrambled information hides and re-emerges · why some
> quantum machine-learning models refuse to train.

This tutorial builds the toolkit once and then follows it across all of them.
By the end you will be able to:

- **average over random unitaries by hand** using the Weingarten calculus, and
  predict second- and fourth-moment quantities (purity, frame potentials,
  gradient variances);
- **read the fingerprints of quantum chaos** in a spectrum — level repulsion,
  the spectral form factor, the random-matrix universality classes;
- **quantify scrambling** with out-of-time-ordered correlators, Krylov
  complexity, and tripartite mutual information;
- **use randomness as a tool** — classical shadows, randomized benchmarking, and
  the Hayden–Preskill recovery protocol;
- **explain barren plateaus** and the expressivity–trainability tension in
  quantum machine learning, from first principles.

## How the tutorial is organized

Seven short parts, each a *concept page* followed by *runnable notebooks*:

| Part | You'll be able to… | Notebooks |
|---|---|---|
| [1 · Mathematical Foundations](chapters/01-foundations.qmd) | Speak the language: channels, Lie algebras, state geometry, measure theory | 14 |
| [2 · Random Matrix Theory](chapters/02-random-matrix-theory.qmd) | Diagnose chaos from a spectrum | 3 |
| [3 · Haar Measure & Weingarten Calculus](chapters/03-haar-weingarten.qmd) | Average over random unitaries and derive the Page formula | 7 |
| [4 · Quantum Dynamics & Chaos](chapters/04-dynamics.qmd) | Measure scrambling in real time | 3 |
| [5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles](chapters/05-designs.qmd) | Replace Haar randomness with something efficient | 2 |
| [6 · Applications of Scrambling](chapters/06-applications.qmd) | Turn randomness into protocols | 5 |
| [7 · Quantum Machine Learning](chapters/07-qml.qmd) | Understand trainability through the same lens | 7 |

You can read it front to back as a course, or jump to any notebook — each one
stands on its own. A companion **[Exercises & Solutions PDF](exercises.qmd)**
collects analytical problems, worked solutions, and flashcards for every part.

## Run it in two minutes

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MarcinPlodzien/quantum-chaos-and-scrambling
cd quantum-chaos-and-scrambling
pip install -r requirements.txt
jupyter lab        # open any notebook under source_notebooks/
```

Everything runs on a laptop with a standard scientific-Python stack
(`numpy`, `scipy`, `matplotlib`). No quantum hardware, no GPUs, no special
libraries.

## Who this is for

Graduate students and researchers in quantum information, condensed matter, or
quantum machine learning — and anyone comfortable with linear algebra and Python
who wants to *compute* with these ideas rather than only read about them. The
mathematical prerequisites are light and built up as needed in Part 1.
